target_year_over_year_context.explanation:
Both disclosures define the methodology for calculating credit risk metrics in the Wealth segment. Specifically, they both state that 90+ days past due delinquency rates are calculated only for the delinquency-managed portfolio, whereas net credit loss rates are calculated using both delinquency and classifiably managed portfolios.

Both disclosures report the Q4 performance trends for the Wealth segment's net credit loss and delinquency rates. The 2024 disclosure notes stability/increases driven by consumer mortgages, while the 2025 disclosure notes decreases/increases driven by California wildfire impacts (forbearance/write-downs). Both address the same specific topic of quarterly credit performance trends for Wealth, albeit with different drivers.

comparisons.peer_summary: Net charge-offs increased $1.2 billion to $3.7 billion in 2024 compared to 2023, while loans 30 days or more past due increased $219 million and those 90 days or more past due increased $177 million at December 31, 2024.
comparisons.comparison: Both C and BAC disclose net credit loss/delinquency metrics for consumer credit products in 2024, but they report divergent trends. C reported that its Q4 2024 net credit loss rate in Wealth was 'broadly stable quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year' while its 90+ day delinquency rate 'increased... primarily driven by consumer mortgages' (c_2024_7_P327_S001, c_2024_7_P327_S002). In contrast, BAC reported that its net charge-offs for the credit card portfolio 'increased $1.2 billion to $3.7 billion in 2024 compared to 2023' and that its 30+ and 90+ day past due loans also increased, indicating a deterioration in credit quality for BAC's credit card portfolio compared to C's stable loss rate and mortgage-driven delinquency increase.

sentences.text: As presented in the chart above, the fourth quarter of 2024 net credit loss rate in Wealth was broadly stable quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year.
The 90+ days past due delinquency rate increased quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year, primarily driven by consumer mortgages.
Net charge-offs increased $1.2 billion to $3.7 billion in 2024 compared to 2023.
Credit card loans 30 days or more past due increased $219 million, and 90 days or more past due increased $177 million at December 31, 2024.

comparisons.peer_summary: Provision for credit losses increased to $1.54 billion in 2024 from $1.14 billion in 2023, primarily driven by net charge-offs in the credit card portfolio.
comparisons.comparison: Both C and GS discuss credit loss metrics and their drivers in 2024, but focus on different portfolio types. C’s Wealth segment reported stable net credit loss rates but rising 90+ day delinquencies driven by consumer mortgages (c_2024_7_P327_S001, c_2024_7_P327_S002). GS reported that its total provision for credit losses increased to $1.54 billion in 2024, with the increase 'primarily [driven] by net charge-offs' in its credit card portfolio (gs_2024_7_P174_S001, gs_2024_7_P174_S002). While C highlights stability in losses despite higher delinquencies in mortgages, GS highlights rising provisions driven by credit card charge-offs.

sentences.text: As presented in the chart above, the fourth quarter of 2024 net credit loss rate in Wealth was broadly stable quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year.
The 90+ days past due delinquency rate increased quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year, primarily driven by consumer mortgages.
Provision for credit losses was $1.54 billion for 2024, compared with $1.14 billion for 2023.
Provisions for 2024 reflected net provisions related to the credit card portfolio (primarily driven by net charge-offs).

comparisons.peer_topic: Credit card portfolio growth and delinquency trends
comparisons.peer_summary: Total credit card loans increased year-over-year due to new accounts and revolving balances. Delinquency rates for 30+ and 90+ days both rose in 2024 compared to 2023, consistent with company expectations.
comparisons.comparison: Both C and JPM disclose trends in credit delinquency and credit loss performance for 2024, but for different loan types. C reported that its 90+ day delinquency rate in Wealth increased, primarily driven by consumer mortgages (c_2024_7_P327_S002). JPM reported that its credit card delinquency rates (both 30+ and 90+ days) also increased in 2024 compared to 2023, rising to 2.17% and 1.14% respectively (jpm_2024_7_P528_S002). While both institutions saw delinquency rates rise, C’s increase was specific to mortgages within Wealth, whereas JPM’s increase was specific to credit cards.

sentences.text: The 90+ days past due delinquency rate increased quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year, primarily driven by consumer mortgages.

The December 31, 2024 30+ and 90+ day delinquency rates of 2.17% and 1.14%, respectively, increased compared to the December 31, 2023 30+ and 90+ day delinquency rates of 2.14% and 1.05%, respectively, in line with the Firm's expectations.
